pos: adj. (the higher of two parts; of a room, a millstone, a spring, a door post, a chamber)
etymology: Comparative of up, Saxon upp. In the Authorized Version upper almost always stands against a stated nether — the upper springs and the nether springs, the upper millstone and the nether — so that the word is never merely a measurement but always one half of a pair.
biblical_def: Upper is a small word that keeps company with large events. The blood of the passover lamb was struck “on the two side posts and on the upper door post of the houses” (Exo 12:7) — three marks, and the upper one over the head of everyone who passed beneath it, so that a household went in and out under the blood. The upper millstone was the turning stone, the one that did the grinding, and the law forbade taking it in pledge because “he taketh a man's life to pledge” (Deu 24:6): a creditor may hold a man's property, but not the instrument by which his household eats. Achsah asked her father for water and received “the upper springs, and the nether springs” (Jos 15:19) — an inheritance measured not in acreage but in water, the whole of a thing rather than the half. And Ahaziah “fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber” (2Ki 1:2) and sent to Baalzebub instead of to the LORD, and died for it. The upper chamber is where the Bible puts its quiet rooms: the widow's loft where Elijah lodged, the room where Christ kept the passover, the room where the hundred and twenty waited. Height in Scripture is never neutral. It is either the place of the blood, the place of the prayer, or the place of the fall.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines upper as higher in place; superior; and the upper millstone as the running or turning stone, the nether being the bedstone.
webster_full: UPPER, a. Higher in place; as the upper lip; the upper story of a house.
1. Superior; higher in power, dignity or station; as the upper ranks of men.
MILLSTONE, n. A stone used for grinding grain. Millstones are used in pairs; the lower or bedstone lies still, and the upper or runner is turned upon it.
NETHER, a. Lower; lying or being beneath, or in the lower part; opposed to upper.
scriptures: Exo 12:7
And they shall take of the blood, and strike it on the two side posts and on the upper door post of the houses, wherein they shall eat it.
Deu 24:6
No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man's life to pledge.
Who answered, Give me a blessing; for thou hast given me a south land; give me also springs of water. And he gave her the upper springs, and the nether springs.

And Ahaziah fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber that was in Samaria, and was sick: and he sent messengers, and said unto them, Go, enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron whether I shall recover of this disease.
corruption_summary: The upper room has been sentimentalized into a mood; Scripture treats it as a place of covenant business.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern devotional imagination has made the upper room a warm and private feeling — an atmosphere of intimacy detached from what actually happened in it. But every upper room in Scripture is a place where something is transacted. The passover is instituted; the Supper is given with the words this is my body and this cup is the new testament in my blood; the eleven wait under a command and are filled. The room is not the point. The covenant enacted in the room is the point, and an upper-room piety that keeps the intimacy while dropping the ordinance has kept the furniture and lost the house.

The principle to recover is that the Authorized Version's ordinary words carry covenant weight. The upper door post is not architectural detail; it is the lintel over which the blood stood between a household and the destroyer. The upper millstone is not agricultural detail; it is the reason a lender may not strip a debtor of the means of life. Read the plain words closely and the law and the gospel are found lying in them.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'elyon (H5945), upper, higher, uppermost; rekeb (H7393), the upper riding stone of a mill; Greek anogeon (G508), an upper chamber or loft.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'elyon (H5945) — upper, uppermost, highest; used of the upper pool, the upper gate, and (capitalized) of God Most High.
Hebrew rekeb (H7393) — the running or upper stone of a hand mill; Deuteronomy 24:6, Judges 9:53.
Hebrew mashqowph (H4947) — the lintel or upper door post on which the passover blood was struck; Exodus 12:7, 12:22-23.
Greek anogeon (G508) — an upper room, a loft; Mark 14:15, Luke 22:12, of the room furnished for the Supper.
Greek huperoon (G5253) — the upper chamber; Acts 1:13, 9:37, 20:8.
usage: “On the upper door post” — the blood stood over the head of every one who went in.
“The upper springs, and the nether springs” — a daughter asked, and a father gave the whole.
“In his upper chamber” — and sent to Ekron rather than to the LORD.

pos: adj. (comparative of high: greater in elevation, in authority, or in kind)
etymology: Comparative of high, Saxon heah. The Authorized Version uses higher in three registers that the reader should keep distinct: physical stature, delegated authority, and the incommensurable difference between God and man.
biblical_def: Higher measures three different things in Scripture, and confusing them is a doctrinal error rather than a reading error. It measures stature: Saul “was higher than any of the people from his shoulders and upward” (1Sa 9:2) — and the man Israel chose by the eye was the man who failed. It measures office: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1), where the magistrate is genuinely above the citizen and yet is himself ordained of God, so that his height is borrowed and answerable. And it measures the distance between the Creator and the creature: “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts” (Isa 55:9). That last is not a difference of degree along one scale; it is the whole reason revelation is necessary. A God whose thoughts were higher by measurement could be reached by climbing. A God whose thoughts are higher as the heavens are higher than the earth must come down or remain unknown. Hence the prayer of the man who has stopped climbing: “lead me to the rock that is higher than I” (Psa 61:2). The refuge is above him, and he asks to be led to it rather than boasting that he has found it. And of Messiah the Father says, “I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth” (Psa 89:27) — the one height that is His by right and not by grant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines high as elevated, lofty, and figuratively as exalted in rank, condition or excellence; higher as its comparative degree.
webster_full: HIGH, a. Extending to a great distance above the surface of the earth; elevated; lofty; of great altitude.
1. Elevated in rank, condition or office; as a high official; the higher powers.
2. Exalted in excellence or extent; as the high attributes of the Deity.
3. Proud; haughty; lofty in an ill sense; as a high look.
scriptures: Isa 55:9
For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.
Psa 61:2
From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth.
corruption_summary: “A higher power” has been emptied into a nameless something; Scripture names Him and names His ways.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase a higher power now circulates as a deliberately unnamed abstraction — a something above me, of no particular character, to which nothing in particular is owed. Scripture never speaks this way. The higher powers of Romans 13 are concrete magistrates with a sword and an account to render; the One whose ways are higher in Isaiah 55 has a name, a covenant, and a summons two verses earlier: let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and let him return unto the LORD. Height in Isaiah is the ground of a call to repent, not a reason to keep the deity vague.

The other corruption runs the opposite way: the assumption that God's higher ways make His revealed word uncertain, so that any hard text may be set aside as unknowable. That reverses the passage. Isaiah says God's thoughts are higher and therefore His word is to be trusted where it speaks — the very next verses promise that the word that goeth forth out of His mouth shall not return void. Transcendence is the guarantee of Scripture's authority, never an excuse for evading it.
roots_summary: Hebrew gabahh (H1361), to be high, exalted; rum (H7311), to be lifted up; Greek huperecho (G5242), to hold above, to be superior.
roots_lines: Hebrew gabahh (H1361) — to be high, tall, lofty; Isaiah 55:9, of the heavens above the earth.
Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, to rise, to be lifted up; used both of God's exaltation and of the proud heart lifted up.
Hebrew tsur (H6697) — rock; Psalm 61:2, the rock that is higher than I.
Greek huperecho (G5242) — to have or hold above, to excel, to be superior; Romans 13:1 (higher powers), Philippians 2:3, 4:7.
Greek hupsistos (G5310) — highest, most high; Luke 2:14, Hebrews 7:1.
usage: “Higher than any of the people” — and Israel chose by the eye.
“The rock that is higher than I” — a man who has stopped climbing.
“So are my ways higher than your ways” — the reason revelation exists.

pos: adj. (comparative of low: beneath in place, in rank, or in glory)
etymology: Comparative of low. In the Authorized Version lower is a word of two very different histories: the humiliation into which Christ descended by choice, and the humiliation into which a proud man is put by another.
biblical_def: “Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour” (Psa 8:5). The psalm says it of man as man — a creature ranked beneath the angels and yet crowned with dominion — and Hebrews takes it up and says it of the Son, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death. That is the deepest use of the word in Scripture: a voluntary lowering, a descent undertaken so that the crown might be given to the very nature that was lowered. The other uses stand around it. Noah's ark had “lower, second, and third stories” (Gen 6:16), a house of salvation built in ranks. The priest examining a plague looked to see whether it lay “lower than the skin” — depth being the mark of a leprosy that had gone in rather than remained upon the surface. Wisdom counsels the guest to take the low seat, “for better it is that it be said unto thee, Come up hither; than that thou shouldest be put lower in the presence of the prince” (Pro 25:7) — the proverb our Lord repeats in Luke 14. And of the enemies of the righteous: “those that seek my soul, to destroy it, shall go into the lower parts of the earth” (Psa 63:9). The whole doctrine of humility is in the difference between going lower and being put lower.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines low as not high or elevated, depressed below the usual level, and humble in condition or rank; lower as its comparative.
webster_full: LOW, a. Not high or elevated; depressed below any given surface or place.
1. Not elevated in rank or condition; humble; as men of low condition.
2. Humble in mind; not proud or aspiring; as a low and contrite spirit.
LOWER, v.t. To let down; to cause to descend; to bring low; to humble.
scriptures: Psa 8:5
For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour.
Pro 25:7
For better it is that it be said unto thee, Come up hither; than that thou shouldest be put lower in the presence of the prince whom thine eyes have seen.
Gen 6:16
A window shalt thou make to the ark, and in a cubit shalt thou finish it above; and the door of the ark shalt thou set in the side thereof; with lower, second, and third stories shalt thou make it.
Psa 63:9
But those that seek my soul, to destroy it, shall go into the lower parts of the earth.
corruption_summary: Lowliness is treated as poor self-regard; Scripture treats it as accurate self-knowledge before God.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage has flattened lowly into a bruised self-image, and the counsel given is therefore to think better of oneself. Scripture never counsels a man to think better or worse of himself as such; it counsels him to think truly, and the truth is that he is a creature made a little lower than the angels, dust by origin and crowned by grace. The lowness commended in Proverbs 25:7 is not a low opinion but a low seat, chosen deliberately by a man who knows he has no claim to the high one. That is why the proverb ends in being called up: God exalts the man who took the honest place.

The second corruption is Christological and older. Because Hebrews applies Psalm 8 to the Son — made a little lower than the angels — some have reasoned from it to a Christ who is lesser in nature than the Father, or an angel Himself. The confessional answer is the state-of-humiliation doctrine: the Son, equal with the Father in essence, took to Himself a true human nature and in it submitted to the law, to suffering and to death, without any subtraction from His deity. He was lowered in state, never in nature.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaphal (H8213), to be low, to be brought low; tachti (H8482), lower, nether; Greek elattoo (G1642), to make less or lower.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaphal (H8213) — to sink, to be humbled, to be brought low; the standing verb behind Isaiah's bringing down of the lofty.
Hebrew tachti (H8482) — lower, nether, lowest; Genesis 6:16 (the lower story), Psalm 63:9 (the lower parts of the earth).
Hebrew me'at (H4592) — a little, a small amount; Psalm 8:5, made a little lower — a measure of degree, and in Hebrews of time.
Greek elattoo (G1642) — to make less, to lower; Hebrews 2:7, 2:9, John 3:30 (I must decrease).
Greek tapeinoo (G5013) — to make low, to humble; Philippians 2:8, He humbled himself.
usage: “A little lower than the angels” — said of man, and then of the Son.
“Lower, second, and third stories” — even the ark of salvation had ranks.
“Put lower in the presence of the prince” — the shame of taking the seat one had not earned.

pos: adj. (comparative of deep: further in, further down, harder to reach or to know)
etymology: Comparative of deep, Saxon deop. Its two great uses in the Authorized Version are diagnostic and doxological: the priest looking to see whether a plague is deeper than the skin, and Zophar asking what a man can know of a wisdom deeper than hell.
biblical_def: The most frequent use of deeper in Scripture belongs to the leprosy law, where it is a diagnostic word: “when the hair in the plague is turned white, and the plague in sight be deeper than the skin of his flesh, it is a plague of leprosy” (Lev 13:3). The priest is trained to ask one question — is this on the surface, or has it gone in? A blemish that lies upon the skin may pass; a plague that lies beneath it defiles. Scripture uses that trained eye everywhere afterward. Sin that has gone in is not managed by scrubbing the surface, and a religion that treats it as surface work is precisely what the prophets and our Lord condemn. The second use lifts the same word to God: “It is as high as heaven; what canst thou do? deeper than hell; what canst thou know?” (Job 11:8). Zophar is a poor comforter, but the sentence is true — the searching out of God is deeper than a creature's line will reach. And Isaiah uses it of judgment by an incomprehensible tongue: “a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive” (Isa 33:19), the Assyrian whose words could not be understood, promised to be seen no more. Three depths, then: the depth of the disease, the depth of God, and the depth of a judgment that speaks in a language you cannot answer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deep as extending far below the surface, descending far downward, and figuratively as profound, not easily fathomed.
webster_full: DEEP, a. Extending or being far below the surface; descending far downward; profound; opposed to shallow.
1. Low in situation; being or descending far below the adjacent land.
2. Not superficial or obvious; hidden; secret; as the deep things of God.
3. Sagacious; penetrating; having the power to enter far into a subject; as a deep divine.
scriptures: Lev 13:3

And the priest shall look on the plague in the skin of the flesh: and when the hair in the plague is turned white, and the plague in sight be deeper than the skin of his flesh, it is a plague of leprosy: and the priest shall look on him, and pronounce him unclean.
Job 11:8
It is as high as heaven; what canst thou do? deeper than hell; what canst thou know?

And if the priest look on the plague of the scall, and, behold, it be not in sight deeper than the skin, and that there is no black hair in it; then the priest shall shut up him that hath the plague of the scall seven days:
Thou shalt not see a fierce people, a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive; of a stammering tongue, that thou canst not understand.
corruption_summary: “Deeper” has become a compliment for the vague; in Scripture it is a word for what is verified, not for what is merely obscure.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary religious speech uses deeper as a term of approval for teaching that is hard to pin down — a deeper truth, a deeper meaning, a deeper reading — where the depth claimed is usually only distance from the text. The priest of Leviticus 13 shows what biblical depth-language actually does: it is a test with a determinate answer, applied by an appointed man, in the light, with a rule. Depth in Scripture is examined, not asserted. The teacher who says his sense is deeper and cannot show it in the words has said nothing.

The genuine depth is the one Zophar names and Paul takes up: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Rom 11:33). It is not a hidden meaning behind the text but the inexhaustible God whom the plain text truly reveals. The right response to it is worship and a closed mouth, not a claim to have sounded it. What is deeper than hell no man can know; what God has written He has written to be understood.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'amoq (H6013), deep, unsearchable; 'amaq (H6009), to be deep, to make deep; Greek bathos (G899), depth.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'amoq (H6013) — deep, mysterious; Leviticus 13 of the plague deeper than the skin, Isaiah 33:19 of a deeper speech.
Hebrew 'amaq (H6009) — to be deep; Job 11:8, deeper than hell (Sheol).
Hebrew she'owl (H7585) — the grave, the unseen state of the dead; the measure of depth in Job's comparison.
Greek bathos (G899) — depth; Romans 11:33 (the depth of the riches of the wisdom of God), 1 Corinthians 2:10 (the deep things of God).
Greek bathuno (G900) — to deepen, to dig deep; Luke 6:48, of the house founded upon a rock.
usage: “Deeper than the skin” — the priest's one question about every plague.
“Deeper than hell; what canst thou know?” — and Zophar was right about that much.
“A deeper speech than thou canst perceive” — judgment in a tongue you cannot answer.

pos: adj. (high, elevated; and of eyes, hearts and cities, proud)
etymology: From loft, the upper room or air; Old Norse lopt, sky, upper chamber. In the Authorized Version lofty is almost always a moral word and almost always about to be brought down — except once, where it belongs to God.
biblical_def: Lofty is Isaiah's word for the thing God has determined to level. “The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day” (Isa 2:11). The day of the LORD is described as a day against everything that stands up: high towers, tall cedars, lifted eyes. “The lofty city, he layeth it low; he layeth it low, even to the ground; he bringeth it even to the dust” (Isa 26:5). Against all of that stands the one place the word is used honorably: “For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit” (Isa 57:15). That verse is the doctrine of the word entire. Loftiness belongs to God alone, by nature and by right; and the God who is genuinely lofty is the God who dwells with the lowly — not because His height is diminished, but because it is not the anxious height of a creature that must defend its place. Hence David's answer at the other end: “LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty” (Psa 131:1). The lofty eye is the visible organ of a proud heart, and Proverbs marks a whole generation by it (Pro 30:13). Lift the eyes and God will lower them; lower them, and God will dwell with you.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lofty as elevated in place, elevated in sentiment or diction, and proud, haughty; and gives the lofty looks of Isaiah as an instance of the last.
webster_full: LOFTY, a. Elevated in place; high; as a lofty tower; a lofty mountain.
1. Elevated in condition or character; as lofty state.
2. Proud; haughty; as lofty looks. Isaiah 2.
3. Elevated in sentiment or diction; sublime; as lofty strains.
scriptures: For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones.
Isa 2:11
The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.
A Song of degrees of David. LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me.
Isa 26:5
For he bringeth down them that dwell on high; the lofty city, he layeth it low; he layeth it low, even to the ground; he bringeth it even to the dust.
corruption_summary: Ambition is now praised as a lofty aspiration; Isaiah calls the lofty look the thing the day of the LORD is against.
corruption_paragraphs: Our age has made lofty a compliment — lofty goals, lofty ambitions — and has thereby lost the one thing Isaiah meant by it. The prophet is not condemning large plans; he is condemning a posture, the lifted eye of a creature who has forgotten whose air he breathes. The test is not the size of the aim but the direction of the gaze. A man may build a great work with lowered eyes, and a man may accomplish nothing at all with lofty ones. The day of the LORD is described as leveling, and what it levels is not achievement but self-exaltation.

The second thing to recover is the astonishing pastoral turn of Isaiah 57:15. The high and lofty One who inhabits eternity does not say that He dwells with the impressive. He names two dwellings and holds them together in one sentence: the high and holy place, and the contrite and humble spirit. That is not divine condescension as a mood; it is the settled character of the God whose loftiness is real. Only a false height needs to keep its distance.
roots_summary: Hebrew gaboahh (H1364), high, lofty, proud; rum (H7311), lifted up; nissa' (H5375), exalted, lifted up — the word of Isaiah 57:15.
roots_lines: Hebrew gaboahh (H1364) — high, lofty; used of towers and of the proud heart alike.
Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be lifted up, exalted; Isaiah 2:11-12, of everything that lifts itself in the day of the LORD.
Hebrew nasa' (H5375) — to lift up, to bear; Isaiah 57:15, the high and lifted up One — the same participle as Isaiah 6:1, high and lifted up upon a throne.
Hebrew dakka' (H1793) — contrite, crushed to powder; the spirit God dwells with in Isaiah 57:15.
Greek hupselos (G5308) — high, lofty; Luke 16:15, that which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God.
usage: “The high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity” — and dwells with the contrite.
“Nor mine eyes lofty” — David naming the organ of pride.
“The lofty city, he layeth it low” — twice, and then to the dust.

pos: adj. (smaller; the inferior of two, chiefly of the moon, of cattle, and of the temple settles)
etymology: A double comparative — less already being comparative — retained in English because the Authorized Version fixed it there. Webster notes the irregularity and keeps the word for its established usage.
biblical_def: “And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night” (Gen 1:16). Moses will not name the sun and moon. The peoples around Israel worshipped them under their names, and the fourth day of creation deliberately reduces them to two lamps and a note that God made the stars also. The lesser light is a governor, and it governs by borrowed light — it has no fire of its own, and its rule over the night is the reflection of a light it does not generate. The church has read the moon this way ever since, and rightly: every derived authority in Scripture — magistrate, elder, husband, father — is a lesser light with a real office and no independent glory. The word appears twice more, in the plain speech of the land and the sanctuary. Isaiah's desolated hill country becomes pasture “for the treading of lesser cattle” (Isa 7:25), sheep and goats grazing where vineyards were. And Ezekiel measures the altar of his temple vision from “the lesser settle even to the greater settle” (Eze 43:14) — the altar rising in ordered ledges, each one measured, the lesser real and necessary and not the greater.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lesser as a barbarous corruption of less, formed by the vulgar from the habit of terminating comparatives in er, but established by usage — less in quantity, degree or dignity.
webster_full: LESSER, a. This word is a corruption; but is authorized by custom, and may be sometimes useful to poetry.
1. Less; smaller; as the lesser light to rule the night. Genesis 1.
LESS, a. Smaller; not so large or great; as a less quantity; a less degree.
1. Inferior in dignity, condition or excellence.
scriptures: Gen 1:16
And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also.
Isa 7:25

And on all hills that shall be digged with the mattock, there shall not come thither the fear of briers and thorns: but it shall be for the sending forth of oxen, and for the treading of lesser cattle.

And from the bottom upon the ground even to the lower settle shall be two cubits, and the breadth one cubit; and from the lesser settle even to the greater settle shall be four cubits, and the breadth one cubit.
corruption_summary: “The lesser of two evils” is treated as a biblical category; Genesis 1 uses the word for a real office under a greater light.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase most people meet the word in — the lesser of two evils — is not a biblical idiom and imports a moral calculus Scripture does not use. The Bible has a category for choosing rightly under constraint, and it is the doctrine of lawful callings and providence, not a scale on which sins are weighed against each other and the lighter one chosen. Where Scripture uses lesser, it is describing something genuinely good that is genuinely subordinate: a light, a herd, a ledge of the altar. The lesser light is not a lesser evil. It is a servant with a station.

The principle to recover is subordination without contempt. Moses could have named the moon and did not; he ranked it. Every derived office in the household of God is a lesser light — deacon under elder, child under parent, wife under husband in the creational order, magistrate under Christ — and the modern instinct is to hear any such ranking as an insult. Genesis 1 hears it as an appointment. The lesser light rules; it simply does not shine on its own.
roots_summary: Hebrew qaton (H6996), small, lesser, younger; ma'or (H3974), luminary, light-bearer; tso'n (H6629), the flock, small cattle.
roots_lines: Hebrew qaton (H6996) — small, little, younger; Genesis 1:16, the lesser (smaller) light.
Hebrew ma'or (H3974) — a luminary, a light-holder; the word Moses uses instead of naming the sun and moon.
Hebrew tso'n (H6629) — flock, small cattle, sheep and goats; Isaiah 7:25.
Hebrew 'azarah (H5835) — a ledge or settle of the altar; Ezekiel 43:14, the lesser and the greater settle.
Greek elasson (G1640) — less, smaller, younger; Romans 9:12, the elder shall serve the younger; Hebrews 7:7, the less is blessed of the better.
usage: “The lesser light to rule the night” — a real rule, on borrowed light.
“The treading of lesser cattle” — vineyards turned to pasture in judgment.
“From the lesser settle even to the greater” — the altar rose in measured ranks.

pos: adj. (first in place or order; the one put in front)
etymology: A double superlative from Saxon forma, first, with the superlative ending added again. Every occurrence in the Authorized Version concerns a man deciding who goes in front of him — and what that decision reveals.
biblical_def: The word occurs three times, and twice in one night. Jacob, hearing that Esau was coming with four hundred men, divided his droves and “commanded the foremost, saying, When Esau my brother meeteth thee…” (Gen 32:17) — sending gift ahead of himself, wave after wave, to appease a brother he had wronged. Then in the morning “he put the handmaids and their children foremost, and Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph hindermost” (Gen 33:2). The order is the plainest confession in Jacob's life: the ones he loved least stood where the danger was, and the ones he loved most stood furthest from it. Scripture reports it without comment and lets the arrangement indict him. Against that stands the shepherd of John 10, who goeth before the sheep, and the Captain of salvation who was made perfect through sufferings — the only leader in Scripture whose foremost position is His own body between the flock and the wolf. The third use is a watchman's: “the running of the foremost is like the running of Ahimaaz” (2Sa 18:27), a man recognized at a distance by his gait — and the news he ran so eagerly to bring was news he had not the courage to tell.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines foremost as first in place, most advanced; and figuratively as first in dignity or importance.
webster_full: FOREMOST, a. First in place; most advanced; as the foremost troops of an army.
1. First in dignity, rank or importance; as the foremost of his profession.
FORE, a. Advanced beyond something else in place; anterior; coming first in order.
scriptures: Gen 33:2
And he put the handmaids and their children foremost, and Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph hindermost.
And he commanded the foremost, saying, When Esau my brother meeteth thee, and asketh thee, saying, Whose art thou? and whither goest thou? and whose are these before thee?
And the watchman said, Me thinketh the running of the foremost is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok. And the king said, He is a good man, and cometh with good tidings.
corruption_summary: Leadership is now measured by visibility in front; Genesis 33 shows a man who put others in front of him.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has become a badge — a foremost authority, foremost in his field — and the biblical uses cut directly against that. Jacob's foremost rank was not the place of honor; it was the place of exposure, and he filled it with the wives and children he valued least. Every leader who arranges his household or his church so that the cost falls on those with the least standing has repeated Genesis 33:2. Scripture does not moralize about it. It simply records the order, and the order is the man.

The corrective is the shepherd who goes before. When he putteth forth his own sheep, he goeth before them (Joh 10:4), and the reason a shepherd goes first is that the danger is first. Christ took the foremost place in that sense and in no other: not the head of the procession but the front of the line where the blow lands. An eldership that understands this will find the foremost position much less attractive and much more necessary.
roots_summary: Hebrew ri'shon (H7223), first, foremost, former; panim (H6440), the face or front; Greek protos (G4413), first.
roots_lines: Hebrew ri'shon (H7223) — first, chief, foremost; Genesis 33:2 of the company placed in front.
Hebrew panim (H6440) — face, front, presence; the root idea behind going before another.
Greek protos (G4413) — first, foremost, chief; 1 Timothy 1:15, of whom I am chief — Paul's only claim to be foremost.
Greek proago (G4254) — to lead forth, to go before; John 10:4, Mark 16:7, the shepherd before the flock.
Greek archegos (G747) — captain, author, one who leads the way; Hebrews 2:10, 12:2.
usage: “He put the handmaids and their children foremost” — and Rachel hindermost.
“He commanded the foremost” — gift after gift, sent ahead of a frightened man.
“The running of the foremost” — a man known by his gait, carrying news he would not tell.

pos: n. and adj. (the exterior surface or part; the outer edge of a camp, a wall, a cup)
etymology: From out and side. The Authorized Version uses it in two settings that interpret each other: the outside of Midian's camp, where Gideon stood in the dark, and the outside of the Pharisee's cup, which he washed while the inside stayed foul.
biblical_def: Our Lord fixed the meaning of this word for the church: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess” (Mat 23:25). The charge is not that they cleaned the outside — the outside of a cup ought to be clean — but that they cleaned only the outside and were content. The remedy He gives is not less washing but a different order: “cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also” (Mat 23:26). Inside-out is the gospel's direction, and it is the reason regeneration precedes reformation in Reformed theology; a new heart produces a clean life, and no amount of scrubbing produces a new heart. Luke records the same words at a Pharisee's table, where our Lord had declined the ceremonial washing before meat (Luk 11:39). The Old Testament uses of outside are literal and set the scene: Gideon “came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch” (Jdg 7:19) with a trumpet, a pitcher and a lamp, and God routed a host with three hundred men who never drew a sword; and Ezekiel's measuring man begins with “a wall on the outside of the house round about” (Eze 40:5), because the holy is bounded, and the first thing a temple has is an edge.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines outside as the external part of a thing; the part, end or side which forms the surface; and figuratively, the superficial appearance.
webster_full: OUTSIDE, n. The external part of a thing; the part, end or side which forms the surface.
1. Superficial appearance; as a fair outside.
2. The utmost; the furthest limit; as, that is the outside of the sum.
SUPERFICIAL, a. Being on the surface; not penetrating the substance of a thing; shallow; contrived to cover something.
scriptures: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess.
Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also.
And the Lord said unto him, Now do ye Pharisees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter; but your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness.
Jdg 7:19

So Gideon, and the hundred men that were with him, came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch; and they had but newly set the watch: and they blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers that were in their hands.
corruption_summary: The cup is still washed on the outside; only the criteria of a clean outside have changed.
corruption_paragraphs: It is easy for a conservative church to read Matthew 23 as a rebuke of somebody else — the ritualist, the legalist, the man with the wrong externals. But the outside of the cup is whatever the surrounding company inspects, and every generation inspects something. Where the marks of belonging are correct opinions, correct alarm at the correct enemies, correct vocabulary, and a presentable family, a man may keep the whole of that outside spotless while extortion and excess sit inside untouched. Our Lord's word is addressed to the most doctrinally careful party of His day, and it lands nearest to those most confident it is not about them.

The order our Lord commands is the whole of the answer, and it is the order of the Reformed ordo salutis: cleanse first that which is within. Regeneration, then repentance and faith, then a life increasingly conformed — the outside genuinely made clean, but made clean second and from within. Any programme that reverses this produces what Matthew 23 describes: whited sepulchres, beautiful outward, and within full of dead men's bones.
roots_summary: Hebrew qatseh (H7097), the end, edge or outside; Greek exothen (G1855), from without, the outside; esothen (G2081), from within.
roots_lines: Hebrew qatseh (H7097) — end, extremity, outside edge; Judges 7:11, 7:17, 7:19, the outside of the armed camp.
Hebrew chuts (H2351) — the outside, the street, that which is without; Ezekiel 40:5.
Greek exothen (G1855) — from outside, the exterior; Matthew 23:25-27, Luke 11:39.
Greek esothen (G2081) — from within, the inward part; the word set against it in the same sentences.
Greek harpage (G724) — extortion, ravening, plunder; what filled the inside of the clean cup.
usage: “Ye make clean the outside of the cup” — and were content with it.
“Cleanse first that which is within” — the order is the doctrine.
“Unto the outside of the camp” — three hundred men, and not a sword drawn.

pos: n. (the hinder part or far side of a thing; in the Authorized Version, of the desert, the tabernacle, and a sealed book)
etymology: From back and side. Plain seventeenth-century English for the rear or reverse of something — the far side of a wilderness, the rear of a tent, the reverse of a scroll.
biblical_def: Three occurrences, and each is a hinge. “Now Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father in law… and he led the flock to the backside of the desert, and came to the mountain of God, even to Horeb” (Exo 3:1). Forty years out of Egypt, at the far end of a wilderness, behind the flock of another man — and that is where the bush burned. God finds Moses at the backside of nowhere, which is the only address at which Moses was fit to be found. The second is the tabernacle's: the extra half curtain of goats' hair “shall hang over the backside of the tabernacle” (Exo 26:12). Even the unseen rear of the dwelling was measured and provided for; God's house has no side that does not matter, and the coverings men would never look at were commanded as precisely as the veil. The third is John's: “a book written within and on the backside, sealed with seven seals” (Rev 5:1). A scroll written on both sides is a scroll that is full — nothing may be added to it — and its seals mean no creature may open it. The tears of Revelation 5 are shed over a history that cannot be read until the Lamb takes the book. The far side of the desert, the far side of the tabernacle, the far side of the scroll: God is at work on the sides no one is looking at.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines backside as the back part of a thing; the hinder part; the part behind, or opposite to the front.
webster_full: BACKSIDE, n. The back part of any thing; the hinder part; that which is behind.
1. The yard or ground behind a house.
BACK, n. The upper or hinder part of an animal; the outer or rear part of any thing; that which is opposite to the face or front.
scriptures: Exo 3:1
Now Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father in law, the priest of Midian: and he led the flock to the backside of the desert, and came to the mountain of God, even to Horeb.
Rev 5:1
And I saw in the right hand of him that sat on the throne a book written within and on the backside, sealed with seven seals.
And the remnant that remaineth of the curtains of the tent, the half curtain that remaineth, shall hang over the backside of the tabernacle.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is plain seventeenth-century English for the rear or reverse of a thing, and modern readers stumble over it only because the noun has since acquired a coarse colloquial sense that the Authorized Version never carries. No doctrine turns on the term.

The principle to recover is providence in obscurity. Every one of the three passages places God's decisive work on the side of things no observer was watching: a shepherd at the far end of a wilderness, a curtain hung where no worshipper would ever see it, writing on the reverse of a sealed scroll. Scripture is unembarrassed by hiddenness, and a believer who measures God's working by what is visible from the front will misread most of his own life. Moses had forty years at the backside of the desert before the bush, and the years were not wasted; they were the preparation.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'achar (H310), behind, the hinder part; yarek (H3411), the rear or flank of a structure; Greek opisthen (G3693), behind, on the back.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'achar (H310) — behind, after, the hinder side; Exodus 3:1, the backside (far side) of the desert.
Hebrew yerekah (H3411) — the rear, the flank, the hindmost part; Exodus 26:12, the back of the tabernacle.
Hebrew Choreb (H2722) — Horeb, the waste; the mountain of God at the desert's far end.
Greek opisthen (G3693) — behind, on the back side; Revelation 5:1, the scroll written within and on the back.
Greek sphragis (G4973) — a seal; seven of them upon the book no man in heaven or earth was found worthy to open.
usage: “The backside of the desert” — and there the bush burned.
“Over the backside of the tabernacle” — measured, though no one would see it.
“Written within and on the backside” — a full scroll, and sealed.

pos: n. (noon; the middle of the day)
etymology: From mid and day, Saxon midd. The Authorized Version's three uses of the word fall on three of the most decisive hours in Scripture: the failure of Baal, the reading of the law, and the conversion of Saul of Tarsus.
biblical_def: “And it came to pass, when midday was past, and they prophesied until the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice, that there was neither voice, nor any to answer, nor any that regarded” (1Ki 18:29). The prophets of Baal had cried from morning, cut themselves with knives and lancets, and leaped upon their altar; midday passed and the heavens were brass. Elijah then repaired the altar of the LORD with twelve stones, prayed a prayer of some sixty words, and fire fell. The hour is part of the argument: a whole bright day of human effort, answered by silence. The second midday is Ezra's: “he read therein… from the morning until midday… and the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the law” (Neh 8:3). Half a day of Scripture read aloud, and a people standing for it — the plainest picture of reformation the Old Testament gives. The third is Paul's: “At midday, O king, I saw in the way a light from heaven, above the brightness of the sun” (Act 26:13). Noon is the brightest hour a man knows, and the glory of the risen Christ outshone it. Every excuse of dimness is answered there. Baal is silent at noon; the word is read at noon; Christ overwhelms the noon sun with His own light.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines midday as the middle of the day; noon; and as an adjective, being at noon, meridional.
webster_full: MIDDAY, n. The middle of the day; noon.
MIDDAY, a. Being at noon; meridional; as the midday sun.
NOON, n. The middle of the day; the time when the sun is in the meridian; twelve o'clock.
scriptures: At midday, O king, I saw in the way a light from heaven, above the brightness of the sun, shining round about me and them which journeyed with me.
And it came to pass, when midday was past, and they prophesied until the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice, that there was neither voice, nor any to answer, nor any that regarded.
Neh 8:3

And he read therein before the street that was before the water gate from the morning until midday, before the men and the women, and those that could understand; and the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the law.
corruption_summary: Conversion is now described as a gradual dawning; Paul dates his to an hour, and the hour was noon.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern testimony language prefers the gradual — a slow opening, a long process, a story with no particular day in it. Scripture allows for that in providence and does not require a datable hour for a true conversion; many are drawn from childhood and could not name the moment. But it flatly refuses to make gradualness the rule. Paul dates his to an hour and a road, and he tells it three times in Acts because the suddenness is part of the evidence: a man on his way to arrest Christians was stopped by the risen Christ at noon. Effectual calling is a work of sovereign grace, and sovereign grace is not obliged to be slow.

The other point to hold is the contest at Carmel. It is fashionable to admire the sincerity of the prophets of Baal — they were earnest, they were costly, they were bleeding. Scripture is unmoved. Earnestness addressed to a god who is not there yields neither voice, nor any to answer, nor any that regarded, and the intensity of the worship does not alter the emptiness of the object. Sincerity is not a saving category; the object of faith is.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsohorayim (H6672), noon, the double light; Greek hemera mese (G2250, G3319), midday; lamprotes (G2987), brightness.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsohorayim (H6672) — noon, midday; a dual form, the double or doubled light of the day's height.
Hebrew machatsith hayyom — the half of the day; Nehemiah 8:3, from the morning until midday.
Greek hemeras meses (G2250 with G3319) — at mid-day; Acts 26:13.
Greek lamprotes (G2987) — brilliance, brightness; the light above the brightness of the sun.
Greek periastrapto (G4015) — to flash around; Acts 9:3, 22:6, the light that shone round about Saul.
usage: “When midday was past” — and there was neither voice nor any to answer.
“From the morning until midday” — and the ears of all the people were attentive.
“At midday… above the brightness of the sun” — noon outshone.
